identity.title: Shoot First, Ask Questions Later? Building Rational Agents that Explore and Act Like People

problem.claim: The paper asks whether language models behave like rational agents when strategically seeking information and acting under uncertainty in high-stakes, resource-limited settings.

gap.claim: The authors report that many language-model agents struggle with informative questioning, accurate answering, and identifying high-utility actions compared with human players.

contributions.claim: Introduces Collaborative Battleship, a decision-oriented dialogue task requiring a Captain to balance questions and shots and a Spotter to provide accurate, context-grounded answers.
Develops Monte Carlo inference strategies for language models inspired by Bayesian Experimental Design to improve agentic information-seeking.
Reports applying the methods beyond Collaborative Battleship to Guess Who?.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe their Monte Carlo inference strategies for language models, inspired by Bayesian Experimental Design, as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that, relative to LM-only baselines, their approach improves Spotter accuracy by up to 14.7 percentage points and Captain expected information gain by up to 0.227 bits, reaching 94.2% of the achievable noise ceiling.
The authors report sharper targeting, with gains of +0.303–0.374 F1, and large win-rate increases for Llama-4-Scout against humans and GPT-5 at approximately 1% of GPT-5’s cost.
On Guess Who?, the authors report accuracy improvements of +28.3–42.4 percentage points and characterize this as evidence of general applicability.

narrative_sequence.summary: Frames strategic information-seeking and tests whether language models act rationally under uncertainty and resource constraints.
Introduces human-cognition-inspired evaluation and the Collaborative Battleship task, separating questioning, answering, and action decisions.
Reports that many language-model agents underperform human players on informative questions, answer accuracy, and action utility.
Presents BED-inspired Monte Carlo inference and reports improvements in answering, information gain, targeting, and competitive win rates.
Reports replication on Guess Who? with substantial accuracy gains.

source_observation.claim: The abstract decomposes information-seeking into distinct roles and measurable behaviors—asking questions, supplying answers, selecting actions, and targeting—and reports component-level gains before combined performance.

lessons.interpretation: This decomposition can make it easier to connect an intervention to the behavior it is intended to improve.
lessons.application: For an agent paper, define separate roles or metrics for information acquisition, belief-relevant answering, action choice, and end-task performance, then report both component and combined results.
lessons.exception: This structure may be unsuitable when the task cannot meaningfully separate information gathering from acting or when role separation changes the task itself.

unknowns: S8–S9 jointly report win-rate increases for weaker LMs such as Llama-4-Scout from 8% to 82% against humans and from 0% to 67% against GPT-5, at approximately 1% of GPT-5's cost; detailed comparison protocols and the cost calculation are not specified in the abstract.
The abstract does not provide experimental protocols, uncertainty estimates, statistical tests, model configurations, or definitions of the achievable noise ceiling and cost calculation.

editorial_revisions.before: S8 is truncated and does not fully specify the comparison or conditions for all reported win rates.
editorial_revisions.after: S8–S9 jointly report win-rate increases for weaker LMs such as Llama-4-Scout from 8% to 82% against humans and from 0% to 67% against GPT-5, at approximately 1% of GPT-5's cost; detailed comparison protocols and the cost calculation are not specified in the abstract.
